fetched_contents.text: Heritage language development in Spanish–English-speaking preschoolers: Influences on growth and challenges in the first year of English-only instruction . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2025 Aug 2. Published in final edited form as: J Child Lang. 2024 Sep 27;52(5):1036–1062. doi: 10.1017/S030500092400045X Abstract This study investigates the changes in the Spanish lexical and grammatical skills of 26 Spanish–English dual language learners during their first year of preschool. We also explore the impact of age, gender, and maternal cultural orientation on children’s language outcomes over time. The results show that, despite one year of English-only instruction, the children’s Spanish productions became more intelligible, lexically diverse, and grammatical between 3;7 and 4;7. However, Spanish productions were mostly limited to sentence fragments and contained errors in grammatical gender, verb morphology, object clitic pronouns, and prepositions. Girls had an advantage over boys, as attested by the higher lexical diversity, mean length of utterance, and grammaticality of their Spanish productions. Both maternal enculturation and acculturation predicted the grammaticality of children’s utterances, suggesting that mothers with high levels of orientation to both Latinx and American culture may be the most successful at promoting Spanish in the United States. Keywords: heritage language development, dual language learners, Spanish, gender, maternal acculturation and enculturation Introduction Immigrant populations across the world are often affected by language shift, a pattern of language use in which the prominence and use of the immigrant community’s native language decrease, leading to an increase in the prominence and use of the societal language (Silva-Corvalán, 1991). Typically, language shift occurs over time and across generations, with the first generation of members from the immigrant group being fluent in their native language but limited in the host country’s language, the second generation being bilingual but dominant in the societal language, and the third generation speaking only the host country’s language. While language shift is gradual and occurs across generations, language use and proficiency changes can also occur within individual speakers and one’s lifespan, in a process called language attrition. Language attrition involves the gradual loss of previously acquired language abilities (Schmid & Köpke, 2009). In the case of young children exposed to both a majority and a minority language, the development of the minority language may stall, resulting in incomplete acquisition compared to monolingual speakers of the target language (Montrul, 2018). Language attrition and incomplete acquisition tend to occur in socio-political contexts characterized by a “minority-majority language dichotomy,” where differing values are attributed, either explicitly or implicitly, to each of these languages (Anderson, 2022, p. 196). This is clearly the case in the United States (US), where the higher-status societal language, English, is not only ever-present in all domains (on the screen, in the street, at school, etc.) but also necessary for professional and educational advancement. Understanding language attrition and incomplete acquisition in contexts where multilingual speakers constitute a large segment of the population is important for educators and policymakers. For instance, in the US – especially its urban areas – many individuals use more than one language daily, and Spanish alone is spoken by over 40 million speakers (www.census.gov). In California, Spanish-speaking Latinx represent nearly one-third of the entire population, and 40% of Los Angeles County residents speak Spanish. In these families, Spanish may be the primary home language; yet children hear both Spanish and English from early on and are formally and consistently exposed to English in preschool or kindergarten, while their Spanish is still being developed. The number of such children in US schools – dual language learners (DLL, Paradis et al., 2021) – has doubled in recent years, and Spanish-speaking children represented 75.5% of all English learners in 2020 (National Center for Education Statistics, 2023). These statistics suggest that Spanish–English DLLs make up a large proportion of students in the classroom, and they may be at risk of attrition or incomplete acquisition of the first (L1) or heritage language (HL) as they are educated in the societal language. Since it has been argued that second language (L2) acquisition is mediated by L1 learning (see Paradis et al., 2021, for a summary), understanding Spanish development among Spanish–English DLLs has significant implications for English language development. Indeed, it has been proposed that as children acquire knowledge and skills in their HL, they also abstract language-independent information that they can apply across learning contexts, a process that may facilitate L2 acquisition (structural sensitivity theory, Kuo & Anderson, 2012; Kuo et al., 2016). This is because, while learning one language, a child acquires a set of skills and knowledge, including conceptual knowledge and syntactic structure, that will support the acquisition of the same concepts and structures in L2. Several studies of young DLLs in different parts of the world have found, indeed, that children who have stronger oral language abilities in their L1 at the beginning of preschool display stronger oral language abilities in their L2 by the end of preschool (Castilla et al., 2009; Grøver et al., 2018; Jackson et al., 2014; Winsler et al., 2014). Introduction In this paper, we investigate Spanish heritage speakers’ accuracy in the comprehension of past aspectual verb forms, specifically the preterite–imperfect contrast, in a context that has not received much attention in the literature thus far: the United Kingdom (UK) (Guardado 2018). Heritage speakers have been proven to be an important source of data for understanding and delimiting the human capacity for language (Lohndal et al. 2019; Polinsky and Scontras 2020) because they are a highly heterogeneous group whose grammatical outcomes typically differ from those of other native speakers of a language. One of the defining characteristics of heritage speakers is that they grow up as bilinguals in a context where their family language is not widely used outside the home (Valdés 2000; Rothman 2009). It is important to note, however, that the UK context is unique and merits careful investigation. In particular, the widespread presence of Spanish as a community language in the United States (USA) (e.g., Pascual y Cabo and de la Rosa Prada 2016) in contact with English over multiple generations may contribute to outcomes observed for Spanish heritage speakers in that context in a way that would not be predicted in the UK (Cazzoli-Goeta and Young-Scholten 2011). Spanish has been claimed to “axiomatically co-exist” with English in the USA (Pascual y Cabo and de la Rosa Prada 2016), reflecting its high visibility as the second most widely spoken language in that country (Lipski 2008), with approximately 17% of the population being of “Hispanic” background (Pascual y Cabo 2018). Silva-Corvalán (1994) noted that whilst Spanish is maintained at the community level in Los Angeles by the constant arrival of new immigrants, the majority of families undergo language shift from Spanish to English, with individuals in the third generation typically functionally reliant on English. More recently, Velázquez (2019) has also documented “low ethnolinguistic vitality” of Spanish in a less urban community, with a similar pattern of the language being maintained at the community level but with families struggling to maintain the Spanish language as their children shift to dominance in English. Spanish heritage speakers, especially adults, have been widely studied in the USA, and these studies have uncovered a high degree of systematic divergence from “expected” linguistic norms throughout this community (see Pascual y Cabo 2018 or Montrul 2018 for recent reviews). By way of contrast, previous research on Spanish speakers in the United Kingdom has highlighted that the community is “present but invisible” (Pozo-Gutiérrez 2003). As such, Spanish–English bilingualism is comparatively less studied in the UK context (Guardado 2018), to the extent that it is difficult to measure with any reliability the number of Spanish L1 speakers or bilinguals within families in the country. Block (2008) reviews demographic and migratory trends and estimates there to be approximately 300,000 Spanish speakers of Latin American origin alone in London, although Paffey (2019) provides a more conservative figure of 190,000 Spanish speakers from both Europe and Latin America in the city. Data from the 2019 Annual Population Survey on country of birth (ONS 2019) indicate that approximately 159,000 Spaniards are resident across the United Kingdom, with an estimated 486,000 residents who were born in Central and South America, although this includes non-Spanish-speaking countries including Caribbean nations, and the 307,000 North Americans in the UK includes Mexicans alongside US citizens and Canadians. Even assuming that all individuals who have migrated to the UK from North, Central and South America are L1 Spanish speakers, this only represents 1.4% of the total UK population, and a more realistic estimate of the Spanish-speaking community in the UK would place this figure below 1%. Guijarro-Fuentes and Marinis (2011) postulate that more favorable attitudes towards bilingualism in the UK may help young Spanish–English bilingual children converge on the baseline, in contrast to observed changes in the grammars of heritage speakers in the USA. Cazzoli-Goeta and Young-Scholten (2011), however, argue that heritage language maintenance amongst Spanish-speaking children in the UK is likely to be minimal due to the lack of a wider speech community. Polinsky (2018) has addressed the question of what constitutes the appropriate baseline for acquisition by heritage speakers, and has argued that different patterns of language change in diaspora and “homeland” communities, and potential attrition in the baseline, may affect the grammatical outcomes of heritage language acquisition. It therefore stands to reason that different patterns of change and attrition may also obtain for diaspora communities in different contexts. To our knowledge, Domínguez (2013) is the only study which explicitly contrasts the outcomes of first-generation L1 Spanish attriters in the USA and UK. Domínguez compared the use of null and post-verbal subjects by L1 Spanish–L2 English speakers living in the UK and in the city of Miami. A large proportion of the population of Miami comes from Cuba, and speak a Caribbean variety of Spanish that has a more rigid Subject-Verb-Object order than other varieties and in which overt subjects are preferred over null subjects more frequently than in other varieties (Ortiz-López et al. 2017). Studies typically define heritage Spanish learners and foreign language learners using a combination of identity, language history, and exposure criteria. Heritage learners are most commonly characterized as individuals who grew up in a home where Spanish was spoken, either because it is their family language or because they were exposed to it early in childhood [N1-R2][N1-R4]. In contrast, foreign language learners are usually defined as students who learned Spanish later in life, often in school or through formal instruction, rather than as a first or heritage language [N1-R1][N1-R4]. A key distinction in the evidence is that heritage language learners are a heterogeneous group, and differences exist between them and foreign language learners [N2-R2][N2-R3].

On measurement, studies often rely on self-report or diagnostic procedures to classify learners, but the evidence here suggests a more cautious approach. For example, the heritage learner definition from CARLA emphasizes that a heritage speaker may speak or merely understand the language, indicating that classification depends on both self-identification and actual linguistic capacity [N1-R2]. The evidence also notes that identifying Spanish heritage speakers involves recognizing diglossia and language standardization issues, suggesting that measures must account for variation in use and proficiency across contexts [N2-R5]. In practice, studies may combine self-reported status with production-based evidence, such as elicited speech or comprehension tasks, to determine whether a learner’s Spanish use is heritage-based or foreign-acquired [N2-R3][N2-R5].

Proficiency and exposure are measured differently across groups. Heritage learners are often assumed to have earlier and more extensive input, even if it is not necessarily fully maintained or practiced later [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Foreign learners, by contrast, are typically assessed through formal classroom performance or standardized tests, which can capture exposure to instruction and current proficiency [N2-R2][N2-R5]. The evidence also indicates that studies frequently control for age of acquisition and other confounding variables, including sociolinguistic context, because heritage and foreign learners differ in when and how they were exposed to the language [N2-R2][N2-R5]. In the cited material, the focus on bilingual environments and language shift underscores that age and exposure interact with acquisition outcomes, so researchers often explicitly report controlling for these factors to isolate the effect of learner status [N2-R3][N2-R5].

Linguistic background and input differences are central to explaining why heritage learners and foreign learners differ in acquisition outcomes. Heritage learners’ input is usually described as early, home-based, and bilingual, whereas foreign learners’ input is typically later, school-based, and often more constrained by instruction and exposure conditions [N4-R3][N4-R4]. The evidence from the heritage language acquisition literature frames acquisition as the growth of a grammatical and communicative system, which implies that input quality and quantity shape grammatical development differently depending on when and how the language is acquired [N4-R1]. In bilingual contexts, heritage speakers do not have identical linguistic competences to monolingual speakers of either the heritage language or the majority language, because their input is shaped by a bilingual environment [N4-R4].

Age of acquisition and exposure are explicitly linked to grammatical development in the evidence. Heritage learners are often younger in acquisition and have longer early exposure, even if later exposure may be reduced or lost over time [N4-R3][N4-R4]. The evidence also points to language shift and attrition, with heritage speakers sometimes developing incomplete acquisition compared to monolingual speakers of the target language [N4-R3]. In the provided material, the discussion of dual language learners and English-only instruction highlights how early exposure interacts with later language use and proficiency [N3-F1]. This suggests that studies control for age and exposure by comparing learners across acquisition timelines and by examining how early bilingual input affects later grammatical performance [N3-F1][N4-R4].

Native language and sociolinguistic context affect complexity performance through input structure, community norms, and language maintenance. The evidence notes that heritage speakers grow up in a context where their family language is not widely used outside the home, which limits input frequency and exposure compared to dominant community languages [N6-F4]. It also emphasizes that different sociolinguistic contexts may produce different attrition or convergence patterns; for example, heritage speakers in the UK are described as “present but invisible,” which affects how their Spanish is maintained and how researchers measure it [N6-F4]. Native language influence is also relevant because the evidence discusses how heritage speakers may display morphosyntactic convergence toward their community’s norms, while foreign learners may show different patterns [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Overall, the evidence supports a model in which acquisition outcomes depend on both the learner’s native linguistic background and the sociolinguistic environment in which the heritage language is used or reduced [N4-R3][N6-F4].

In experimental and corpus work, learner status is operationally distinguished through a mixture of self-report, diagnostic, and production-based procedures. The evidence shows that researchers often start with self-reported status, because heritage learners are defined as individuals raised in homes where a non-English language is spoken and who may speak or merely understand the language [N1-R2][N1-R4]. However, self-report alone is not sufficient, because the literature explicitly warns that heritage speakers are a heterogeneous group and that differences exist between them and foreign language learners [N2-R2][N2-R3]. As a result, studies frequently combine self-report with diagnostic or production-based measures to confirm status [N2-R5].

Self-reported data are used to identify learner status, but they are treated cautiously. The evidence indicates that identifying Spanish heritage speakers requires recognizing diglossia and language standardization issues, suggesting that self-report must be supplemented by more direct evidence [N2-R5]. In practice, studies may use elicited speech, comprehension tasks, or written responses to assess whether a learner’s Spanish is heritage-based or foreign-acquired [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The material also points to diagnostic procedures, such as comprehension of tense-aspect morphology, as a way to distinguish learners and test grammatical knowledge [N6-F4]. In corpus work, the intersection of heritage language studies and corpus linguistics is emphasized, implying that large-scale production data are used alongside more controlled elicitation [N7-R3][N7-R4].

Mixed-status or ambiguous cases are handled by researchers through explicit classification and control strategies. The evidence suggests that mixed-status groups are recognized as a challenge because heritage learners are heterogeneous, and studies may therefore report separate heritage and foreign learner subgroups or use mixed-status controls [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The same evidence also notes that studies must account for bilingual environments and language shift, which implies that ambiguous cases are resolved by comparing performance across groups rather than collapsing them into a single category [N4-R4]. In the provided material, the emphasis on identifying heritage speakers and on controlling for language shift and attrition suggests that ambiguous cases are managed through careful grouping and explicit reporting of status criteria [N2-R5][N4-R4].

The grammatical features most frequently examined in Spanish acquisition studies are tense-aspect, mood, agreement, and morphosyntactic structures more generally. The evidence is explicit that heritage speakers often display erosion and loss of the tense-aspect and mood system in oral production, and that comprehension studies examine past aspectual verb forms, especially the preterite-imperfect contrast [N6-F3][N6-F4]. Morphosyntactic features are also central, with studies discussing morphosyntactic convergence, subject-object expression, and the acquisition of Spanish morphosyntax [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-F2]. The broader literature also highlights that Spanish learners’ morphosyntax is a major focus of acquisition research, covering both verbal and nominal domains [N5-F2].

Each feature is operationalized through experimental or corpus tasks designed to elicit and measure grammatical knowledge. For tense-aspect, the evidence includes comprehension tasks and semantic interpretation tasks, in which bilinguals or heritage speakers are asked to interpret tense-aspect morphology [N6-F4][N8-R3]. For agreement and morphosyntactic features, studies use elicited production, written responses, and diagnostic tasks to assess grammatical knowledge [N2-R3][N6-F4]. The evidence also mentions that corpus research methods are used alongside experimental approaches, which means that production data can be analyzed across large corpora to examine frequency and usage patterns [N7-R3][N7-R4]. In morphosyntax, the evidence points to studies on subjunctive/syntax development and on subject and object expression, indicating that features are often operationalized as production errors, comprehension accuracy, or grammatical structure use [N5-R3][N5-R5].

Studies compare performance across learners and features by contrasting heritage speakers with foreign language learners and by examining how different grammatical properties develop. The evidence shows that heritage speakers are compared with L2 learners or bilinguals in studies on tense-aspect comprehension, and that performance differences are interpreted as evidence of heritage status [N6-F3][N6-F4]. Similarly, the morphosyntactic literature compares different learner groups and reports on how features such as agreement and morphology vary across acquisition stages [N5-R2][N5-F2]. The evidence also indicates that studies use mixed-status groups and controls to separate effects of learner status from effects of the specific grammatical feature [N2-R2][N4-R4]. Overall, the most common pattern is to measure performance on a feature, then compare it across heritage and foreign learners while controlling for age, exposure, and sociolinguistic context [N5-F2][N6-F4].

Studies infer learner status from performance on complex grammatical features by treating certain features as diagnostic of heritage versus foreign learner status. The evidence repeatedly identifies tense-aspect, mood, agreement, and morphosyntactic structures as the most diagnostic areas. In particular, heritage speakers are shown to display erosion and loss of the tense-aspect and mood system in oral production, while comprehension studies examine past aspectual verb forms and the preterite-imperfect contrast [N6-F3][N6-F4]. Morphosyntactic features such as subject-object expression, agreement, and subjunctive/syntax development are also central, with studies noting that heritage speakers may show morphosyntactic convergence or error patterns distinct from foreign learners [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-F2]. Because these features are highly visible in production and comprehension tasks, they are the most commonly used indicators of learner status in the evidence [N6-F3][N6-F4][N5-F2].

Performance differences are interpreted as evidence of heritage status when heritage speakers show systematic divergence from expected norms, especially in morphosyntactic and tense-aspect systems. The evidence states that heritage speakers often display erosion and loss in oral production and that their grammatical outcomes typically differ from those of other native speakers of the language [N6-F3][N6-F4]. In comparative studies, heritage speakers are contrasted with L2 learners or bilinguals, and differences in accuracy, comprehension, or production are read as evidence of heritage status rather than merely of proficiency [N6-F4][N8-R3]. The evidence also shows that studies compare heritage speakers with foreign learners across features such as tense-aspect comprehension, subject-object expression, and agreement, reinforcing the idea that feature performance is used to distinguish the two groups [N6-F3][N6-F4][N5-R2]. In corpus work, production data are similarly used to identify patterns that align with heritage speaker norms [N7-R3][N7-R4].

Limitations and confounds include the possibility that performance differences reflect exposure, proficiency, age of acquisition, or sociolinguistic context rather than heritage status itself. The evidence explicitly notes that heritage learners are heterogeneous and that differences exist between them and foreign language learners, so a single feature result cannot reliably distinguish heritage from foreign learners without controlling for other variables [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The upstream reports also emphasize that studies often control for age of acquisition, exposure, and sociolinguistic context because these variables shape grammatical development differently [N9][N12]. Another limitation is that self-report or diagnostic procedures may not fully capture ambiguous status, so studies must rely on mixed-status controls or separate groups to avoid conflating status with other confounding factors [N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-R4]. Additionally, the evidence suggests that sociolinguistic context can influence convergence or attrition, so a feature may appear “heritage-like” because of community norms rather than because the learner is a heritage speaker [N6-F4][N12]. Overall, the studies infer learner status from performance cautiously, treating complex grammatical features as diagnostic but recognizing that interpretation depends on controlling for exposure, proficiency, age, and sociolinguistic variation [N6-F3][N6-F4][N9][N12].

## Integrated synthesis of how studies distinguish heritage Spanish learners from foreign language learners in acquisition of complex grammatical features

Studies distinguish heritage Spanish learners from foreign language learners by combining operational definitions, methodological controls, and performance comparisons on complex grammatical features. The distinction is not merely about whether someone speaks Spanish, but about when, how, and in what context the language was acquired, and how that history affects grammatical development [N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N4-R4].

### 1. How studies define and measure heritage versus foreign learners

Heritage Spanish learners are typically defined as individuals who grew up in a home where Spanish was spoken, either because it is their family language or because they were exposed to it early in childhood [N1-R2][N1-R4]. In contrast, foreign language learners are usually defined as students who learned Spanish later in life, often in school or through formal instruction, rather than as a first or heritage language [N1-R1][N1-R4]. A central point in the evidence is that heritage learners are a heterogeneous group, and differences exist between them and foreign language learners [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This means that definitions must account for identity, language history, and exposure rather than relying on a single marker [N2-R5].

Proficiency and exposure are measured differently across groups. Heritage learners are often assumed to have earlier and more extensive input, even if that input is not necessarily fully maintained or practiced later [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Foreign learners, by contrast, are typically assessed through formal classroom performance or standardized measures that reflect exposure to instruction and current proficiency [N2-R2][N2-R5]. The evidence also shows that studies control for age of acquisition and other confounding variables because heritage and foreign learners differ in when and how they were exposed to the language [N2-R2][N2-R5]. This is important because the timing and quality of exposure shape grammatical development differently [N9].

### 2. How learner status is operationally distinguished in experimental and corpus work

In experimental and corpus work, learner status is operationally distinguished through a mixture of self-report, diagnostic, and production-based procedures. Researchers often start with self-reported status, because heritage learners are defined as individuals raised in homes where a non-English language is spoken and who may speak or merely understand the language [N1-R2][N1-R4]. However, self-report alone is not sufficient, because the literature explicitly warns that heritage speakers are a heterogeneous group and that differences exist between them and foreign language learners [N2-R2][N2-R3]. As a result, studies frequently combine self-report with diagnostic or production-based measures to confirm status [N2-R5].

Self-reported data are used to identify learner status, but they are treated cautiously. The evidence indicates that identifying Spanish heritage speakers requires recognizing diglossia and language standardization issues, suggesting that self-report must be supplemented by more direct evidence [N2-R5]. In practice, studies may use elicited speech, comprehension tasks, or written responses to assess whether a learner’s Spanish is heritage-based or foreign-acquired [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The material also points to diagnostic procedures, such as comprehension of tense-aspect morphology, as a way to distinguish learners and test grammatical knowledge [N6-F4]. In corpus work, the intersection of heritage language studies and corpus linguistics is emphasized, implying that large-scale production data are used alongside more controlled elicitation [N7-R3][N7-R4].

Mixed-status or ambiguous cases are handled by researchers through explicit classification and control strategies. The evidence suggests that mixed-status groups are recognized as a challenge because heritage learners are heterogeneous, and studies may therefore report separate heritage and foreign learner subgroups or use mixed-status controls [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The same evidence also notes that studies must account for bilingual environments and language shift, which implies that ambiguous cases are resolved by comparing performance across groups rather than collapsing them into a single category [N4-R4]. In the provided branch reports, this is reinforced by the emphasis on controlling for exposure, proficiency, and sociolinguistic context [N9][N10].

### 3. Which grammatical features are most commonly studied

The grammatical features most frequently examined in Spanish acquisition studies are tense-aspect, mood, agreement, and morphosyntactic structures more generally. The evidence is explicit that heritage speakers often display erosion and loss of the tense-aspect and mood system in oral production, and that comprehension studies examine past aspectual verb forms, especially the preterite-imperfect contrast [N6-F3][N6-F4]. Morphosyntactic features are also central, with studies discussing morphosyntactic convergence, subject-object expression, and the acquisition of Spanish morphosyntax [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-F2]. The broader literature also highlights that Spanish learners’ morphosyntax is a major focus of acquisition research, covering both verbal and nominal domains [N5-F2].

### 4. How each feature is operationalized in experimental or corpus tasks

Each feature is operationalized through experimental or corpus tasks designed to elicit and measure grammatical knowledge. For tense-aspect, the evidence includes comprehension tasks and semantic interpretation tasks, in which bilinguals or heritage speakers are asked to interpret tense-aspect morphology [N6-F4][N8-R3]. For agreement and morphosyntactic features, studies use elicited production, written responses, and diagnostic tasks to assess grammatical knowledge [N2-R3][N6-F4]. The evidence also mentions that corpus research methods are used alongside experimental approaches, which means that production data can be analyzed across large corpora to examine frequency and usage patterns [N7-R3][N7-R4]. In morphosyntax, the evidence points to studies on subjunctive/syntax development and on subject and object expression, indicating that features are often operationalized as production errors, comprehension accuracy, or grammatical structure use [N5-R3][N5-R5].

### 5. How studies compare performance across learners and features

Studies compare performance across learners and features by contrasting heritage speakers with foreign language learners and by examining how different grammatical properties develop. The evidence shows that heritage speakers are compared with L2 learners or bilinguals in studies on tense-aspect comprehension, and that performance differences are interpreted as evidence of heritage status [N6-F3][N6-F4]. Similarly, the morphosyntactic literature compares different learner groups and reports on how features such as agreement and morphology vary across acquisition stages [N5-R2][N5-F2]. The evidence also indicates that studies use mixed-status groups and controls to separate effects of learner status from effects of the specific grammatical feature [N2-R2][N4-R4]. Overall, the most common pattern is to measure performance on a feature, then compare it across heritage and foreign learners while controlling for age, exposure, and sociolinguistic context [N5-F2][N6-F4].

### 6. How linguistic background and input differences affect acquisition outcomes

Linguistic background and input differences are central to explaining why heritage learners and foreign learners differ in acquisition outcomes. Heritage learners’ input is usually described as early, home-based, and bilingual, whereas foreign learners’ input is typically later, school-based, and often more constrained by instruction and exposure conditions [N4-R3][N4-R4]. The evidence frames acquisition as the growth of a grammatical and communicative system, which implies that input quality and quantity shape grammatical development differently depending on when and how the language is acquired [N4-R1]. In bilingual contexts, heritage speakers do not have identical linguistic competences to monolingual speakers of either the heritage language or the majority language, because their input is shaped by a bilingual environment [N4-R4].

Age of acquisition and exposure are explicitly linked to grammatical development in the evidence. Heritage learners are often younger in acquisition and have longer early exposure, even if later exposure may be reduced or lost over time [N4-R3][N4-R4]. The evidence also points to language shift and attrition, with heritage speakers sometimes developing incomplete acquisition compared to monolingual speakers of the target language [N4-R3]. In the branch reports, the discussion of dual language learners and English-only instruction highlights how early exposure interacts with later language use and proficiency [N3-F1]. This suggests that studies control for age and exposure by comparing learners across acquisition timelines and by examining how early bilingual input affects later grammatical performance [N3-F1][N4-R4].

Native language and sociolinguistic context affect complexity performance through input structure, community norms, and language maintenance. The evidence notes that heritage speakers grow up in a context where their family language is not widely used outside the home, which limits input frequency and exposure compared to dominant community languages [N6-F4]. It also emphasizes that different sociolinguistic contexts may produce different attrition or convergence patterns; for example, heritage speakers in the UK are described as “present but invisible,” which affects how their Spanish is maintained and how researchers measure it [N6-F4]. Native language influence is also relevant because the evidence discusses how heritage speakers may display morphosyntactic convergence toward their community’s norms, while foreign learners may show different patterns [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Overall, the evidence supports a model in which acquisition outcomes depend on both the learner’s native linguistic background and the sociolinguistic environment in which the heritage language is used or reduced [N4-R3][N6-F4].

### 7. How studies infer learner status from performance on complex grammatical features

Studies infer learner status from performance on complex grammatical features by treating certain features as diagnostic of heritage versus foreign learner status. The evidence repeatedly identifies tense-aspect, mood, agreement, and morphosyntactic structures as the most diagnostic areas. In particular, heritage speakers are shown to display erosion and loss of the tense-aspect and mood system in oral production, while comprehension studies examine past aspectual verb forms and the preterite-imperfect contrast [N6-F3][N6-F4]. Morphosyntactic features such as subject-object expression, agreement, and subjunctive/syntax development are also central, with studies noting that heritage speakers may show morphosyntactic convergence or error patterns distinct from foreign learners [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-F2]. Because these features are highly visible in production and comprehension tasks, they are the most commonly used indicators of learner status in the evidence [N6-F3][N6-F4][N5-F2].

Performance differences are interpreted as evidence of heritage status when heritage speakers show systematic divergence from expected norms, especially in morphosyntactic and tense-aspect systems. The evidence states that heritage speakers often display erosion and loss in oral production and that their grammatical outcomes typically differ from those of other native speakers of the language [N6-F3][N6-F4]. In comparative studies, heritage speakers are contrasted with L2 learners or bilinguals, and differences in accuracy, comprehension, or production are read as evidence of heritage status rather than merely of proficiency [N6-F4][N8-R3]. The evidence also shows that studies compare heritage speakers with foreign learners across features such as tense-aspect comprehension, subject-object expression, and agreement, reinforcing the idea that feature performance is used to distinguish the two groups [N6-F3][N6-F4][N5-R2]. In corpus work, production data are similarly used to identify patterns that align with heritage speaker norms [N7-R3][N7-R4].

Limitations and confounds include the possibility that performance differences reflect exposure, proficiency, age of acquisition, or sociolinguistic context rather than heritage status itself. The evidence explicitly notes that heritage learners are heterogeneous and that differences exist between them and foreign language learners, so a single feature result cannot reliably distinguish heritage from foreign learners without controlling for other variables [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The upstream reports also emphasize that studies often control for age of acquisition, exposure, and sociolinguistic context because these variables shape grammatical development differently [N9][N12]. Another limitation is that self-report or diagnostic procedures may not fully capture ambiguous status, so studies must rely on mixed-status controls or separate groups to avoid conflating status with other confounding factors [N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-R4]. Additionally, the evidence suggests that sociolinguistic context can influence convergence or attrition, so a feature may appear “heritage-like” because of community norms rather than because the learner is a heritage speaker [N6-F4][N12]. Overall, the studies infer learner status from performance cautiously, treating complex grammatical features as diagnostic but recognizing that interpretation depends on controlling for exposure, proficiency, age, and sociolinguistic variation [N6-F3][N6-F4][N9][N12].

### Bottom line

In short, studies distinguish heritage Spanish learners from foreign language learners in acquisition of complex grammatical features by:  
1) defining learners through identity, language history, and exposure [N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3];  
2) measuring proficiency and exposure separately for each group [N1-R1][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R5];  
3) controlling for age, exposure, and sociolinguistic context [N9][N12];  
4) using a mix of self-report, diagnostic, and production-based procedures to identify learner status [N2-R3][N2-R5][N7-R3][N7-R4];  
5) focusing on tense-aspect, mood, agreement, and morphosyntactic features as the most commonly studied areas [N6-F3][N6-F4][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-F2];  
6) operationalizing features through comprehension, elicited production, and corpus analysis [N6-F4][N8-R3][N7-R3][N7-R4];  
7) interpreting performance differences as evidence of heritage status, but only after accounting for confounding factors [N6-F3][N6-F4][N9][N12].

This approach reflects a broader methodological trend in heritage language research: treat learner status as a multidimensional construct that cannot be reduced to one feature alone, and use complex grammatical performance as a window into how acquisition, input, and sociolinguistic context interact [N2-R2][N4-R4][N6-F4][N12].

Studies distinguish heritage Spanish learners from foreign language learners by combining operational definitions, methodological controls, and performance comparisons on complex grammatical features. The distinction is not merely about whether someone speaks Spanish, but about when, how, and in what context the language was acquired, and how that history affects grammatical development [N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R2][N2-R3][N4-R4].

### 1. How studies define and measure heritage versus foreign learners

Heritage Spanish learners are typically defined as individuals who grew up in a home where Spanish was spoken, either because it is their family language or because they were exposed to it early in childhood [N1-R2][N1-R4]. In contrast, foreign language learners are usually defined as students who learned Spanish later in life, often in school or through formal instruction, rather than as a first or heritage language [N1-R1][N1-R4]. A central point in the evidence is that heritage learners are a heterogeneous group, and differences exist between them and foreign language learners [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This means that definitions must account for identity, language history, and exposure rather than relying on a single marker [N2-R5].

Proficiency and exposure are measured differently across groups. Heritage learners are often assumed to have earlier and more extensive input, even if that input is not necessarily fully maintained or practiced later [N1-R1][N1-R4]. Foreign learners, by contrast, are typically assessed through formal classroom performance or standardized measures that reflect exposure to instruction and current proficiency [N2-R2][N2-R5]. The evidence also shows that studies control for age of acquisition and other confounding variables because heritage and foreign learners differ in when and how they were exposed to the language [N2-R2][N2-R5]. This is important because the timing and quality of exposure shape grammatical development differently [N9].

### 2. How learner status is operationally distinguished in experimental and corpus work

In experimental and corpus work, learner status is operationally distinguished through a mixture of self-report, diagnostic, and production-based procedures. Researchers often start with self-reported status, because heritage learners are defined as individuals raised in homes where a non-English language is spoken and who may speak or merely understand the language [N1-R2][N1-R4]. However, self-report alone is not sufficient, because the literature explicitly warns that heritage speakers are a heterogeneous group and that differences exist between them and foreign language learners [N2-R2][N2-R3]. As a result, studies frequently combine self-report with diagnostic or production-based measures to confirm status [N2-R5].

Self-reported data are used to identify learner status, but they are treated cautiously. The evidence indicates that identifying Spanish heritage speakers requires recognizing diglossia and language standardization issues, suggesting that self-report must be supplemented by more direct evidence [N2-R5]. In practice, studies may use elicited speech, comprehension tasks, or written responses to assess whether a learner’s Spanish is heritage-based or foreign-acquired [N2-R3][N2-R5]. The material also points to diagnostic procedures, such as comprehension of tense-aspect morphology, as a way to distinguish learners and test grammatical knowledge [N6-F4]. In corpus work, the intersection of heritage language studies and corpus linguistics is emphasized, implying that large-scale production data are used alongside more controlled elicitation [N7-R3][N7-R4].

Mixed-status or ambiguous cases are handled by researchers through explicit classification and control strategies. The evidence suggests that mixed-status groups are recognized as a challenge because heritage learners are heterogeneous, and studies may therefore report separate heritage and foreign learner subgroups or use mixed-status controls [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The same evidence also notes that studies must account for bilingual environments and language shift, which implies that ambiguous cases are resolved by comparing performance across groups rather than collapsing them into a single category [N4-R4]. In the provided branch reports, this is reinforced by the emphasis on controlling for exposure, proficiency, and sociolinguistic context [N9][N10].

### 3. Which grammatical features are most commonly studied

The grammatical features most frequently examined in Spanish acquisition studies are tense-aspect, mood, agreement, and morphosyntactic structures more generally. The evidence is explicit that heritage speakers often display erosion and loss of the tense-aspect and mood system in oral production, and that comprehension studies examine past aspectual verb forms, especially the preterite-imperfect contrast [N6-F3][N6-F4]. Morphosyntactic features are also central, with studies discussing morphosyntactic convergence, subject-object expression, and the acquisition of Spanish morphosyntax [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-F2]. The broader literature also highlights that Spanish learners’ morphosyntax is a major focus of acquisition research, covering both verbal and nominal domains [N5-F2].

### 4. How each feature is operationalized in experimental or corpus tasks

Each feature is operationalized through experimental or corpus tasks designed to elicit and measure grammatical knowledge. For tense-aspect, the evidence includes comprehension tasks and semantic interpretation tasks, in which bilinguals or heritage speakers are asked to interpret tense-aspect morphology [N6-F4][N8-R3]. For agreement and morphosyntactic features, studies use elicited production, written responses, and diagnostic tasks to assess grammatical knowledge [N2-R3][N6-F4]. The evidence also mentions that corpus research methods are used alongside experimental approaches, which means that production data can be analyzed across large corpora to examine frequency and usage patterns [N7-R3][N7-R4]. In morphosyntax, the evidence points to studies on subjunctive/syntax development and on subject and object expression, indicating that features are often operationalized as production errors, comprehension accuracy, or grammatical structure use [N5-R3][N5-R5].

### 5. How studies compare performance across learners and features

Studies compare performance across learners and features by contrasting heritage speakers with foreign language learners and by examining how different grammatical properties develop. The evidence shows that heritage speakers are compared with L2 learners or bilinguals in studies on tense-aspect comprehension, and that performance differences are interpreted as evidence of heritage status [N6-F3][N6-F4]. Similarly, the morphosyntactic literature compares different learner groups and reports on how features such as agreement and morphology vary across acquisition stages [N5-R2][N5-F2]. The evidence also indicates that studies use mixed-status groups and controls to separate effects of learner status from effects of the specific grammatical feature [N2-R2][N4-R4]. Overall, the most common pattern is to measure performance on a feature, then compare it across heritage and foreign learners while controlling for age, exposure, and sociolinguistic context [N5-F2][N6-F4].

### 6. How linguistic background and input differences affect acquisition outcomes

Linguistic background and input differences are central to explaining why heritage learners and foreign learners differ in acquisition outcomes. Heritage learners’ input is usually described as early, home-based, and bilingual, whereas foreign learners’ input is typically later, school-based, and often more constrained by instruction and exposure conditions [N4-R3][N4-R4]. The evidence frames acquisition as the growth of a grammatical and communicative system, which implies that input quality and quantity shape grammatical development differently depending on when and how the language is acquired [N4-R1]. In bilingual contexts, heritage speakers do not have identical linguistic competences to monolingual speakers of either the heritage language or the majority language, because their input is shaped by a bilingual environment [N4-R4].

Age of acquisition and exposure are explicitly linked to grammatical development in the evidence. Heritage learners are often younger in acquisition and have longer early exposure, even if later exposure may be reduced or lost over time [N4-R3][N4-R4]. The evidence also points to language shift and attrition, with heritage speakers sometimes developing incomplete acquisition compared to monolingual speakers of the target language [N4-R3]. In the branch reports, the discussion of dual language learners and English-only instruction highlights how early exposure interacts with later language use and proficiency [N3-F1]. This suggests that studies control for age and exposure by comparing learners across acquisition timelines and by examining how early bilingual input affects later grammatical performance [N3-F1][N4-R4].

Native language and sociolinguistic context affect complexity performance through input structure, community norms, and language maintenance. The evidence notes that heritage speakers grow up in a context where their family language is not widely used outside the home, which limits input frequency and exposure compared to dominant community languages [N6-F4]. It also emphasizes that different sociolinguistic contexts may produce different attrition or convergence patterns; for example, heritage speakers in the UK are described as “present but invisible,” which affects how their Spanish is maintained and how researchers measure it [N6-F4]. Native language influence is also relevant because the evidence discusses how heritage speakers may display morphosyntactic convergence toward their community’s norms, while foreign learners may show different patterns [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Overall, the evidence supports a model in which acquisition outcomes depend on both the learner’s native linguistic background and the sociolinguistic environment in which the heritage language is used or reduced [N4-R3][N6-F4].

Studies infer learner status from performance on complex grammatical features by treating certain features as diagnostic of heritage versus foreign learner status. The evidence repeatedly identifies tense-aspect, mood, agreement, and morphosyntactic structures as the most diagnostic areas. In corpus work, production data are similarly used to identify patterns that align with heritage speaker norms [N7-R3][N7-R4].

In short, studies distinguish heritage Spanish learners from foreign language learners in acquisition of complex grammatical features by:
